title: Tisha B'Av: Lamentations
hookLine: read by candlelight, sitting low; the Talmud says the second Temple fell for baseless hatred (Yoma 9b)

cards: Evening, in a synagogue, on the ninth of Av. The big lights are off or turned low. In many places the curtain has been taken down from the ark.
People wear sneakers or cloth shoes, because leather is set aside for the day. Nobody greets anyone. They sit on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at home.
Someone has a candle, someone a phone flashlight. Then a reader begins a slow, falling chant, and the first word is a cry.

teach.b: Eicha means how, the how you say when you can't believe what you're seeing. It's the first word of Lamentations, and Jews call the whole book by it. The old Jewish translation opens: "How doth the city sit solitary."
Jerusalem, once full of people, sits alone like a widow. Of the book's five chapters, four are built on the alphabet, verse by verse, as if grief needed every letter there is.

teach.h: TWO TEMPLES, ONE DAY OF MOURNING.
teach.b: Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the day the tradition remembers both Temples falling, the first to Babylon, the second to Rome, centuries apart, mourned on one day. It's a full fast, from sunset to the next nightfall.
Anyone who is ill, pregnant, nursing, or whose health would be at risk asks a doctor and a rabbi, and Jewish law puts protecting life first. Then the mourner's question: why?
The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, gives a stinging answer. The first Temple fell because of idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed.
But in the second Temple's time, people studied Torah, kept the commandments and did acts of kindness. So why did it fall?
Sinat chinam, baseless hatred: hatred for no reason worth the name.
And baseless hatred, it says, weighs as much as those three sins together.
The rabbis didn't only blame the empire with the battering rams. They looked at their own community: the feuds, the contempt, the neighbor nobody would speak to. And the book doesn't end in the dark.
Its last chapter asks God to turn us back and renew our days as of old, and because the very last verse is so bitter, the congregation says that line again.

how: On Tisha B'Av many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations chanted in a dim synagogue, followed by kinot, poems of mourning.

o: woe: the shofar blast that ends the fast day
how: the cry that opens and names Lamentations
ruins: a name for the Temple's fallen stones

s: the Talmud says the second Temple fell because people stopped studying Torah
Yoma 9b says they studied, kept the commandments and did kindness; it fell for baseless hatred.
four of Lamentations' five chapters follow the alphabet
verse by verse, from the first letter to the last.
both Temples are mourned on the same day
the ninth of Av remembers the fall of the first and of the second.

games.q: you're a sage after the second Temple burned. the people studied and kept the commandments. why did it fall?
games.why: the Talmud (Yoma 9b) says baseless hatred, and that it weighs as much as idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed together.

practice: If you can, sit low, on the floor or a step, and let one grudge come to mind, the kind that isn't about anything big anymore: an old slight, a neighbor you decided long ago not to like.
You don't have to forgive the unforgivable or call anyone; just, for this minute, set this one down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor.

wordCard.voice: Eicha. How: the first word and the Hebrew name of Lamentations, read on Tisha B'Av, sitting low. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: how. the first word of Lamentations, and its Hebrew name.

carryVoice: Your line: baseless hatred destroys. A day on the floor, asking why out loud. Until tomorrow.
